title: What Aggregate Scores Hide: Group Baselines for Fine-Grained Claims
abstract: A probe R², a judge-human agreement rate or a cross-validated correlation is often read as evidence of fine-grained structure. When the target is grouped, a predictor that knows only the group can attain such a score. Building on conditional probing (Hewitt et al., 2021), we compare selected published headlines H with training-only group baselines B in the paper's own metric and, for nested comparisons, quantify the conditional predictive gain (CPG): the out-of-sample reduction in squared error from adding the representation to the group predictor, split exactly into group-mean and within-group parts. The aim is to quantify what a published score allows one to infer about the resolution of prediction. In our worked example, the space and time probes of Gurnee & Tegmark, country, state or borough means match or exceed the published space scores, and resolution oracles built from the target exceed the time scores. Beyond country and state means, residual readouts from four 6-7B models remove 20-34% of the remaining coordinate error (an increase in total R² of .008-.013); for one of them the CPG point estimates met thresholds frozen before evaluation, although with whole countries resampled the World interval reaches zero. On the eligible USA subset with counties observed in training, the saved readouts' net gain over state means comes from between-county differences, and a cross-fitted linear recalibration within counties yields gains near zero. Below the century, decade or year the gains are small. The same diagnostic applies to a language-model probe of political ideology, a Twitter prediction of county heart-disease mortality and LLM judges: on retained non-tie votes, a model-identity baseline calibrated from other human votes in the same collection attains much of the judges' agreement with humans, while the judges reduce its disagreement rate by 12-28%. We recommend reporting both numbers, at more than one grouping level, whenever a salient grouping could plausibly attain much of the reported performance.

title: Sentiment analysis in rural areas: a systematic review of applications and approaches
abstract: Rural depopulation and territorial imbalances are ongoing challenges that require innovative tools for understanding community needs and informing evidence-based policy. Sentiment Analysis (SA) has emerged as a promising methodology for extracting emotional information from large volumes of digital text data. However, despite its growing methodological relevance across the social sciences, its application to rural contexts is limited, and no prior systematic review has examined the application of SA within rural research. This article aims to assess the usefulness and potential of SA in rural research through a systematic review of existing applications and a critical analysis of its methodological contributions. The systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Eligible studies applied SA to textual or social media data and focused on rural areas or explicitly compared rural and urban contexts. Searches were performed in Scopus and Web of Science (WOS) up to March 2025. A total of 47 studies were included and analysed. Data extraction was performed from the reviewed studies, collecting information on the location, study type, authors’ discipline, and methodological quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) and a consensus review by the research team. Key results were extracted, including areas of application of SA, methodologies employed, and data sources. Additionally, a thematic analysis was conducted considering the main areas of application of SA and its limitations. The studies reveal a developing field where SA is increasingly applied across various domains, particularly in rural tourism and public health, as well as in agriculture, food policy and social well-being. A significant geographic concentration of research is observed in China and the United States. The studies employ various SA processing methodologies (lexicon-based, machine learning, deep learning and hybrid approaches) and diverse data sources (social media, surveys, digital reviews). Methodological quality was generally high, with 85% of the studies scoring 7 or higher on the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Furthermore, the analysis identified notable differences in perceptions between rural and urban areas, emphasizing the importance of considering local contexts in public policy discussions. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the role of SA in rural development and offer valuable insights for future research and policy formulation aimed at addressing the specific needs of rural communities.

title: A method for multimodal analysis of TAIGA experiment data using essential features
abstract: The aim of processing and analyzing experimental data from physical experiments is to obtain physically significant information about the phenomenon under study. This goal is achieved by multi-stage processing of experimental data, during which noise associated with measurements is suppressed and the dimensionality of the input data is reduced. In this paper, we propose a new method based on the use of neural networks such as autoencoders to extract essential features. The special value of the proposed approach lies in the possibility of its application to the analysis of multimodal data received simultaneously from several installations. We will apply this approach to a multimodal data (MMD) of the experiment TAIGA. Currently, the analysis of the MMD is carried out independently for each installation separately. Therefore, the development of methods for the joint analysis of MMD from TAIGA-type installations is an urgent task in cosmic ray physics and gamma-ray astronomy. Based on Monte Carlo simulation, it is shown that the proposed method allows for effective MMD analysis. It can also be used for MMD analysis at other experimental complexes.

title: Efficiently computable bounds on the energy-constrained quantum reading capacity
abstract: In quantum reading, classical messages are encoded in sequences of quantum channels and recovered by probing the channels and processing their outputs. We study the reading capacity of a finite family of finite-dimensional channels under an average constraint on the probing energy, allowing arbitrary adaptive operations between channel uses. Using an input-dependent chain rule for the Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy, we derive a converse bound expressed as an optimization involving channel Choi operators and the operator relative entropy. This formulation admits semidefinite approximations and reduces, without an energy constraint, to a channel information radius. To obtain achievable rates, we construct bilinear semidefinite lower approximations to a standard non-adaptive reading bound. Alternating optimization produces feasible probe states and encoding distributions, whose Holevo information gives a directly evaluable achievable rate. For jointly classical-quantum channels, we derive a separate converse based on the Umegaki relative entropy. Without an energy constraint, this converse matches a non-adaptive achievable rate, recovering a recent result of Pascual Abraldes and Winter: non-adaptive protocols suffice to achieve the unconstrained reading capacity of jointly classical-quantum channels.

title: LiDAR Resolution Recovery via Foundation-Model-Guided Diffusion
abstract: High-beam-count LiDAR sensors are costly, yet many perception pipelines require dense angular sampling. Using a pretrained Stable Diffusion model as the backbone, we fine-tune a LiDAR-conditioned depth model with pseudo-depth targets from a 2D foundation model. During training, the LiDAR conditioning is randomly decimated at different beam budgets. We then investigate how much of a LiDAR scan can be recovered from heavily decimated input and characterize performance across the input beam budget. We evaluate against physically held-out real beams on nuScenes and report recovery separately from fit accuracy. Our model yields its largest advantage in very sparse regimes, achieving a $δ_{1.25}$ accuracy of $66.8$% from $4$-beam input where scattered interpolation reaches only $45.1$%. A class-stratified error breakdown further reveals that planar surfaces recover first while objects introducing depth discontinuities degrade earliest. Together, these results quantify the recovery/resolution trade-off for foundation-model-guided LiDAR enhancement.

title: M3SunAgent: Monocular 3D Spatial Understanding Agent for Metric Depth Estimation and 3D Visual Grounding
abstract: Monocular metric depth estimation and 3D visual grounding represent the two complementary cornerstones of monocular 3D spatial understanding (M3Sun), from which the fundamental 3D spatial information required by M3Sun can be acquired. However, these complementary tasks are generally conducted by separate frameworks, which pose challenges of inflexible and unaligned spatial information access for embodied intelligence systems. In this paper, we propose a unified agent for monocular 3D spatial understanding (M3SunAgent) that leverages a large language model (LLM) as a task planner for spatial visual programming, which flexibly generate structured programs and coordinate tools. For instance-level metric depth estimation task, M3SunAgent invokes an object detector tool to locate the target, estimates depth at selected points with a depth estimation tool, and aggregates these predictions into an instance-level depth estimate. We also construct the M3Sun Instance (M3SI) dataset, a benchmark with 2,910 samples for evaluation. For monocular 3D visual grounding task, M3SunAgent uses a vision-language model (VLM) tool to locate the target and output basic spatial attributes, then combines back-projection tool with a dimension-lifting tool to predict its 3D bounding box. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of M3SunAgent. Specifically, in evaluations of instance-level monocular metric depth estimation, M3SunAgent achieves the best performance among all compared models, 52.61% of predicted instances are distributed below depth error 0.25 ($δ< 0.25$). In evaluations of monocular 3D visual grounding, M3SunAgent demonstrates overall competitive performance than vision and VLM models, reaching a 3D mean intersection over union (mIoU) of 41.73% and exceeding the state-of-the-art MonoVLM model by 3.62%.

title: HUMAN-AI COEVOLUTION FOR NEURAL DISCOVERY AT THE LIMIT AI Candidate Generation, Human Scientific Judgment & Persistent Research Memory
abstract: HUMAN-AI COEVOLUTION FOR NEURAL DISCOVERY AT THE LIMITAI Candidate Generation, Human Scientific Judgment & Persistent Research Memory This flagship volume explores a future of neural science in which the cost of generating hypotheses, couplings, countermodels, literature syntheses, experimental sketches, and research pathways falls dramatically. In such an environment, the limiting resource is no longer the production of candidate ideas. The bottleneck becomes scientific selection: deciding which questions deserve attention, which candidates are genuinely testable, which evidence is trustworthy, which risks are acceptable, which paths should stop, and which research memories must survive model and institutional turnover. The book is organized around a three-coupling: AI Candidate Generation x Human Scientific Judgment x Persistent Research Memory. Its book-defined heuristic is HAEN = (A_g x H_j x P_m x R_d) / (1 + F_v + A_b + O_c). The equation is a conceptual research architecture, not a natural law or validated clinical metric. It is used to reason about a research system in which machine generation expands the option space, human judgment retains direction and responsibility, evidence adjudicates empirical claims, and persistent memory preserves why the research changed. A central scientific boundary runs throughout the work: AI fluency, generation volume, self-consistency, and internal agreement are not validation. Candidate generation and scientific selection must remain separable. A model can propose ten thousand elegant couplings and still produce no scientific knowledge if those candidates cannot be operationalized, falsified, externally tested, or compared against simpler alternatives. Neural science raises the stakes because measurement error, proxy leakage, automation bias, stale memory, and authority creep can become persuasive interpretations about cognition, communication, health, or intervention. The 82 chapters develop eight linked domains: candidate generation and search-space design; rival hypotheses and adversarial review; evidence retrieval and source stratification; human direction and responsibility interfaces; AI disagreement as a search signal; persistent research memory and lineage; high-risk neural AI authority envelopes; and joint handoff to successor agents. The architecture treats AI not as a second pen but as an auditable candidate generator, critic, retrieval partner, and memory participant. Human scientists retain the ability to choose direction, request rivals, reject attractive but weak claims, reduce scope, and stop high-risk pathways. The volume also develops a practical idea for disagreement. When models disagree, the preferred response is not immediate averaging or rhetorical debate. Disagreement should be classified and converted into a discriminating experiment. Competing hypotheses are therefore preserved as versioned families with explicit evidence states, predicted differences, and next tests. Failure is retained as negative knowledge rather than deleted from the lineage. Persistent research memory is treated as more than conversation history. A mature system should remember candidate versions, semantic definitions, evidence provenance, rejected branches, human decisions, consent state, authority envelopes, stop conditions, and the reasons for every major transition. Successor AI systems should inherit methods for changing answers, not a frozen archive of inherited conclusions. High-risk neural AI receives a deliberately narrow authority model. Prediction is not permission to intervene. Data access is not permission to expand purpose. New inference capability is not automatic authorization under old consent. Human override, dynamic consent, cognitive liberty, mental privacy, psychological integrity, revocation, and exitability are treated as engineering constraints inside the research system. After the 82 chapters, 200 Research Gates transform unresolved questions into structured research spaces. Each Gate contains a three-coupling, core question, research move, evidence boundary, success signal, failure or falsification signal, authority or stop condition, and handoff note. The book then closes with 33 Answer Embryos designed around a phoenix cycle: Question -> Provisional Model -> Test -> Breakdown -> Recombination -> Rebirth. These embryos are not final answers. They are provisional structures intended to be tested, rejected, split, merged, and rebuilt. The deeper proposition is simple: as AI makes generation abundant, direction becomes more valuable. The future of human-AI science may depend less on who can generate the most candidates and more on who can preserve evidence discipline, meaningful disagreement, human authority, persistent memory, and successor freedom. A mature research system should not merely produce more possibilities. It should remain navigable, auditable, reversible, and worth inheriting.

title: CHATBOT DE ATENDIMENTO: UTILIDADE OU SATISFAÇÃO? UMA ANÁLISE DA PERCEPÇÃO DA COMUNIDADE ACADÊMICA DA UNIOESTE – TOLEDO/PR.
abstract: O ambiente de negócios tem sido transformado pelas tecnologias digitais que redefiniram a forma como empresas e consumidores interagem. Este estudo tem como objetivo avaliar a percepção da comunidade acadêmica da Unioeste de Toledo/PR quanto à utilidade e satisfação no uso de chatbots de atendimento e assistentes virtuais. Para coleta de dados foi elaborado um questionário com questões predominantemente objetivas, incluindo afirmativas na escala de Likert de 5 pontos. Ao total obteve-se 41 respondentes, incluindo docentes, discentes e agentes universitários. Os resultados apontam que os entrevistados aceitam o chatbot e assistente virtual como uma possibilidade de atendimento, contudo essa aceitação é feita com ressalva, pois aspectos como segurança, empatia, resolução de problemas de forma personalizada ainda representam pontos de tensão na percepção deles.

evidence.title: CHATBOT DE ATENDIMENTO: UTILIDADE OU SATISFAÇÃO? UMA ANÁLISE DA PERCEPÇÃO DA COMUNIDADE ACADÊMICA DA UNIOESTE – TOLEDO/PR.
evidence.abstract: O ambiente de negócios tem sido transformado pelas tecnologias digitais que redefiniram a forma como empresas e consumidores interagem. Este estudo tem como objetivo avaliar a percepção da comunidade acadêmica da Unioeste de Toledo/PR quanto à utilidade e satisfação no uso de chatbots de atendimento e assistentes virtuais. Para coleta de dados foi elaborado um questionário com questões predominantemente objetivas, incluindo afirmativas na escala de Likert de 5 pontos. Ao total obteve-se 41 respondentes, incluindo docentes, discentes e agentes universitários. Os resultados apontam que os entrevistados aceitam o chatbot e assistente virtual como uma possibilidade de atendimento, contudo essa aceitação é feita com ressalva, pois aspectos como segurança, empatia, resolução de problemas de forma personalizada ainda representam pontos de tensão na percepção deles.

title: OBAN k-flow: code and results for exact minimum sound and complete evidence certificates in retrieval-augmented generation
abstract: Code and complete experimental outputs for the manuscript "OBAN k-flow: Exact minimum sound and complete evidence certificates for retrieval-augmented generation" (V. Oban, submitted to Information Processing & Management). OBAN k-flow selects the smallest set of retrieved passages that is both sound (every atomic claim of a fixed answer is supported through an admissible witness hypergraph) and complete (every relevant omitted passage is dominated by the selected ones in a capacitated maximum-flow network), and returns a dual-bound proof of minimality from a single mixed-integer program. The package contains: code/: certification engine (witness hypergraph, two-sided MILP with SciPy/HiGHS, independent max-flow recheck), the SciFact and HotpotQA pipeline (BM25, dense, hybrid RRF and cross-encoder retrieval, extractive reader, NLI verification), statistical analysis, report generation, the Kaggle notebooks used for the experiments, and oracle tests against exhaustive enumeration; results/: recorded verifier scores and all certificates for three NLI verifiers (DeBERTa-v3 base and large cross-encoders), with and without the relevance gate, plus per-query analysis outputs; report/: all result tables (Excel), a Word report and the attribution and verifier-comparison summaries. Licence: code under MIT; results under CC BY 4.0. Claims, questions and answers taken from SciFact and HotpotQA remain under the licences of their original releases.

title: PREreview of "VeriHarness: Scaling Agentic Verification for Long-Horizon Tasks"
abstract: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23180223. ## Summary As agents take on long-horizon work — reports, spreadsheets, multi-file artifacts — checking their outputs becomes the bottleneck. This paper studies verification under the hardest honest constraint: no stronger judge exists, so the verifier must use the same model as the generator, with no access to reference answers or grading rubrics. The central empirical finding is striking: when you sample many rollouts of the same task, agreement among them does not reliably mean correctness. On ten-rollout pools from Claude Opus 4.8, about a third of the values all rollouts agreed on were judged wrong, while three-quarters of disputed claims contained a correct candidate somewhere — and the most common answer was right less than half the time. Majority voting is therefore not just weak; it actively preserves errors. VeriHarness turns the generator's own model into an agentic verifier with a workspace, evidence tools, and reusable verification skills: a disagreement resolver that tests competing claims against source files, and a consensus challenger that proposes ways the shared consensus could be wrong. The system is training-free and plug-and-play, achieves the highest selection scores among baselines across five workspace benchmarks and two frontier models, and releases ~26,000 rollouts (produced at over $100,000 in compute) for future research. ## Strengths The "consensus can conceal errors" finding should change default practice — roughly 34% of unanimous values wrong is a refutation of the sample-and-vote recipe, not a rounding error. The same-model constraint is the honest setting: showing gains with the same weights means the improvement comes from the harness and the environment, a much more deployable claim. The verification record (every claim linked to its check, evidence, and verdict) turns verification into training signal. The skill-evolution result — evolved-from-empty skills outperforming human-authored ones on held-out tasks — suggests verification know-how can be accumulated rather than hand-coded. Releasing a $100K rollout corpus is a real community contribution. ## Major concerns and questions 1. What does verification cost? The harness runs a resolver, a challenger, and an adjudicator — each an agentic loop with tool calls — on top of N generator rollouts. If verification costs 3-5x the generation it protects, the economics only work for high-stakes artifacts. A cost-per-verified-task analysis is the missing number that determines whether this is deployable or academic. 2. Correlated blind spots are the core risk of same-model verification: if the generator misreads a source document, the verifier with the same weights may misread it the same way. On the subset of tasks where the verifier fails, how often is the failure a shared misreading versus a checking error? That decomposition would reveal whether the harness is hitting a correlated-error floor. 3. The headline statistics come from one model on one benchmark (Claude Opus 4.8 on APEX-Agents). A small table of these statistics across all ten model-benchmark cells would materially strengthen the paper's foundation. 4. All five benchmarks produce document artifacts — the friendliest setting for evidence-based verification. A discussion of where the claim-level formalism breaks (multi-turn tool-use, emergent code behavior) would help readers scope the contribution. 5. Skill evolution: if the dev set is narrow, the evolved library may be memorizing benchmark-specific patterns. Cross-benchmark-family transfer (evolve on A, test on B) would be the convincing test. ## Overall assessment An important paper with a genuinely practice-changing core finding. The same-model constraint makes the results honest, and the two-check decomposition is the right abstraction. The missing pieces are cost accounting and a direct measurement of the correlated-error floor — both addressable, both needed before teams should deploy this. **Verdict: Recommend with revisions.** Competing interests The author declares that they have no competing interests. Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) The author declares that they used generative AI to come up with new ideas for their review.
